questiontext.text:
Take the four consecutive integers to be \(n\), \(n + 1\), \(n + 2\) and \(n + 3\), where \(n\) is an integer. Show that the product of the last two minus the product of the first two equals the sum of all four.

Work line by line in the box. The first line, \((n + 2)(n + 3) - n(n + 1)\), is typed for you. Start each new line with =, expand and simplify, and finish with the sum written out, \(n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) + (n + 3)\). Type products as n*(n+1) or n(n+1).

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Expand both products, collect terms, and compare with the sum. Each line is equal to the one before:

\[\begin{aligned}(n + 2)(n + 3) - n(n + 1) &= n^2 + 5n + 6 - n^2 - n\\ &= 4n + 6\\ &= n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) + (n + 3).\end{aligned}\]

The minus sign in front of \(n(n + 1)\) applies to both of its terms: \(-n(n + 1) = -n^2 - n\). So for any four consecutive integers, the product of the last two minus the product of the first two equals the sum of all four. Writing the integers as \(n - 1\), \(n\), \(n + 1\), \(n + 2\) gives \(4n + 2\) for both.

Other chains are just as good, for example one that passes through \(2(2n + 3)\) instead of \(4n + 6\). What matters is that every line equals the one before, and that at least one line of working comes between the first line and the sum.

questiondescription.text: This question is adapted from Exercise 4, p. 26, in Section 6 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022: the algebra of the proof is written as a chain of equal expressions, checked line by line.

node.description: Each line equals the one before
Some working comes between the first line and the sum (the first new line is not the sum itself)

falsefeedback.text: Every line is equal to the one before, but the working jumps to the answer. Expand both products and collect terms, so that the reader can see that the difference simplifies to the same expression as the sum.

node.description: The chain ends with the sum written out

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="hasval"]]

Your chain shows \((n + 2)(n + 3) - n(n + 1) = 4n + 6 = n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) + (n + 3)\), which proves the statement.

[[else]]

Your chain shows \((n + 2)(n + 3) - n(n + 1) = n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) + (n + 3)\), which proves the statement. Both expressions simplify to \(4n + 6\).

[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="nowork"]]

There is no working yet. Start a new line with =, expand both products and collect terms.

[[else]]

Your working is correct so far. To finish the proof, end with the sum itself, \(n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) + (n + 3)\), so that the chain shows that the difference equals the sum.

[[/if]]

truefeedback.text: Each line marked ? is not equal to the line before it. When you subtract \(n(n + 1)\), the minus sign applies to both terms: \(-n(n + 1) = -n^2 - n\).

falsefeedback.text: Each line marked ? is not equal to the line before it. Expand each product carefully, and put the second product in brackets before you subtract it.
